mcqs.question: `const rabbit = Object.create(animal); rabbit.hops = true;` — later, `animal.eats` is changed to `false`. What does `rabbit.eats` return afterward?
options: Whatever `animal.eats` was at the moment `Object.create` ran, since it's copied at creation
true, because own properties always take priority over inherited ones
false — the new value, because `rabbit` looks the property up through the live prototype link on every access
undefined, because changing a prototype property after creation breaks the link
mcqs.explanation: The prototype link isn't a one-time copy — every property read walks the chain fresh, so `rabbit.eats` reflects `animal.eats`'s current value. `rabbit` has no own `eats` property to take priority, and changing the prototype's property doesn't sever the link.

options: Both live on `Dog.prototype`, shared across every instance
Both live directly on `rex` as own properties
`bark` lives once on `Dog.prototype`, shared by every instance; `name` is an own property set on `rex` itself by the constructor
`name` lives on `Dog.prototype`; `bark` is copied onto each instance when `new` runs
mcqs.explanation: `new Dog(...)` links the new object's prototype to `Dog.prototype` and runs the constructor body, which sets `this.name` as an own property on the new instance. `bark` was only ever assigned once, onto `Dog.prototype`, so it's found via the chain rather than duplicated per instance.

mcqs.question: After `rex.bark = function() { return "quiet"; }`, is `Dog.prototype.bark` changed for other `Dog` instances?
options: Yes, because assigning to `rex.bark` always updates the prototype it inherited from
No — assigning to `rex.bark` creates a new own property on `rex` that shadows the prototype method; `Dog.prototype.bark` is untouched and other instances still use it
Yes, but only if `rex` was created with `Object.create` instead of `new`
No, because functions on a prototype cannot ever be shadowed by an instance
mcqs.explanation: Setting a property on an instance always creates or overwrites an own property on that instance — it never reaches up the chain to mutate the prototype. Other instances keep using `Dog.prototype.bark` unaffected; shadowing is entirely possible and is exactly what happened here.

mcqs.question: A codebase mutates `Dog.prototype` at runtime, adding a new method, after several `Dog` instances already exist. What happens to those existing instances?
options: Nothing — their prototype link was fixed permanently at the moment they were constructed
They immediately gain access to the new method too, because their prototype link points to the same live `Dog.prototype` object
They throw an error the next time any method is called on them
Only instances created after the mutation can see the new method
mcqs.explanation: The prototype link is a live reference to the same object, not a snapshot taken at construction time — so mutating `Dog.prototype` is visible to every instance linked to it, past or future, on their very next lookup. This is impossible in a true compile-time class model, which is the point of contrasting the two mental models.

options: [] — each instance gets its own empty array
["Alice"] — both instances share the same array via the prototype link, so `a`'s mutation is visible on `b`
undefined, because `push` detaches the array from the prototype
A TypeError, because prototype properties are read-only
mcqs.explanation: `Team.prototype.members` is one array shared by every instance through the prototype chain. `push` mutates that single array in place rather than creating a new one or an own property on `a`, so `b.members` sees the same change. The fix is assigning `this.members = []` inside the constructor instead.

mcqs.question: Why do engines like V8 recommend initializing all of an object's properties in the constructor, in a consistent order, across every instance of a type?
options: It has no real performance effect — it's purely a stylistic convention
It reduces the number of properties JavaScript allows an object to have
It's required by the `class` syntax, though not by plain constructor functions
Consistent shapes let the engine reuse the same hidden class and cached lookups across instances; adding or deleting properties later creates new hidden classes and can de-optimize hot code
mcqs.explanation: Engines optimize property access by tracking an object's shape (hidden class) and caching lookups against it — instances with the same shape share that optimization. Objects that gain or lose properties after construction, or build them in a different order, force new hidden classes and lose the fast path. It's a real performance effect, not a syntax requirement or a hard property-count limit.
